chunks: When a man swears an oath upon something, and that which he has sworn upon — doing it is better than leaving it, then let him do that which is better, and there is no expiation upon him. Rather, that is from the footsteps of Satan.

key_terms.إِتْيَانُهُ: Doing it / fulfilling it; the act of carrying out what was sworn
key_terms.حَلَفَ: Swore an oath (yameen); a binding verbal commitment in Islamic law
key_terms.خُطُوَاتِ الشَّيْطَانِ: Footsteps of Satan; a Quranic phrase (2:168, 6:142) signifying following the path of evil
key_terms.كَفَّارَةَ: Expiation (kaffarah); the ritual compensation required for breaking certain oaths

ai.seo_question: If fulfilling an oath leads to harm, is there expiation required for breaking it in Shia Islam?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) issues a jurisprudential ruling that when a person's oath would lead to a worse outcome than breaking it, he should choose the better action without incurring any expiation (kaffarah). The Imam frames stubborn oath-keeping at the cost of doing good as a satanic impulse, referencing the Quranic phrase 'footsteps of Satan' to warn that rigid literalism in oaths can itself be a form of moral corruption. This ruling reflects the Islamic principle that oaths are not meant to bind a person to harm.
